query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A short-duration sub-critical anneal of heavily cold-rolled AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy at around 800–900 °C for approximately 15–30 minutes will induce a partially recrystallized, refined hierarchical lamellar microstructure that simultaneously increases both yield strength and ductility relative to the cold-rolled or fully annealed baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Heavily cold-rolled AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy
generation.intervention: A controlled, single-step sub-critical annealing at 800–900 °C for roughly 15–30 minutes
generation.conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests performed at ambient temperature on specimens in the partially recrystallized condition
generation.structural_mediator: Partially recrystallized, hierarchical lamellae (combination of recovered B2 regions and refined L12/FCC grains)
generation.mechanism: The preservation of fine lamellar constraints combined with partially recrystallized grains increases the density of dislocation storage sites while enhancing strain hardening and delaying crack initiation, thereby strengthening the alloy and maintaining or improving ductility compared to cold-rolled or fully annealed states.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a fully annealed or as-cold-rolled baseline, yield strength is expected to exceed ~1.2–1.3 GPa while elongation to failure remains ~10–15%, showing a net gain in both strength and ductility over the baseline.
generation.baseline: Cold-rolled AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with negligible elongation or fully annealed EHEA with lower yield strength
generation.boundary: Excessive annealing times or higher temperatures may lead to coarse microstructures, reducing the benefits of the refined partial recrystallization. The effect applies primarily to lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs under moderate to high plastic strain conditions before annealing.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimal annealing temperatures, times, and cooling rates may be alloy-dependent and require further experimental validation for upscaling.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three batches of heavily cold-rolled AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA samples. Subject one batch to the proposed sub-critical annealing method (e.g., 850 °C for 15–30 min), keep one batch in the as-cold-rolled condition, and fully anneal the last batch. Perform microstructure characterization (TEM/SEM) and uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature on all batches.
measurements: Grain size distribution and fraction of recrystallized microstructure (via TEM/EBSD).
Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the partially annealed samples fail to exhibit both a measurable increase in yield strength over fully annealed samples and a higher elongation relative to the as-cold-rolled samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. decision.trend: Early work (PMC4145285) established lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEAs with excellent strength-ductility combinations in the as-cast state. Subsequent studies (PMC5818523, PMC6353877, PMC6687781) showed that refining and modifying these lamellar microstructures through multi-step thermomechanical processing (e.g., cryo-rolling followed by short annealing, or sequential cold + warm rolling) yields even better strength-ductility synergy. The main successes relied on introducing hierarchical, ultrafine lamellae or dual-phase microstructures to activate multiple deformation mechanisms, but practical routes to achieve reproducible, consistent improvements for larger-scale components remain a challenge.
decision.unsolved: Despite clear enhancements from complex rolling-plus-annealing processes, a reliable single-step intervention for controlling and optimizing lamellar refinement and phase distribution in EHEAs is not yet well established, especially for larger-scale production. Ensuring thermal stability and replicating these promising strength-ductility combinations for bulk structural components remain open issues.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled, short-duration sub-critical annealing (e.g., 800–900 °C for ~15–30 minutes) of heavily cold-rolled AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to induce partial recrystallization and form a refined, hierarchical lamellar microstructure.
decision.why: Building on prior results where multi-step cryo-/warm rolling and partial recrystallization led to improved ductility and strength, a single-step sub-critical annealing can stabilize ultrafine lamellae and a dual-phase distribution. This single intervention should enhance dislocation storage while preserving some lamellar constraints, thereby boosting yield strength and ductility simultaneously.
